faqs.q: An opossum has moved in under my Remington porch — is that a problem?
faqs.a: A passing opossum eating snails and fallen fruit is harmless, but one denning under a porch or in a crawlspace in Remington fouls the space and will be reused by the next animal. Opossums are not a rabies-vector species here, despite the fierce display when cornered. Our crew removes the animal at the property under permit, cleans the den area, and seals the gap it used.

faqs.q: After the river comes up, animals get under our Remington house. Why?
faqs.a: High water evicts everything living in the river bottom at once — skunks, opossums, and raccoons all move uphill in the same few days, and the first dry, dark voids they find are crawlspaces and porch foundations in town. If your foundation vents are open or your porch is unskirted, you are on their list every flood. We remove whoever has moved in, then screen the vents and skirt the porches with buried wire so the next high water finds your house closed — that screening is the whole difference between a one-time job and a flood-season subscription.

faqs.q: Woodchucks are under our equipment shed out past Remington. Worth removing?
faqs.a: If the shed matters, yes. A woodchuck system under a slab or a dirt-floored shed removes the soil holding it up, run by run, and the shed floor usually announces the problem by cracking or settling. We remove the resident animals, collapse and backfill the burrow runs, and screen the perimeter so the system is not re-claimed — empty burrows in Fauquier farm country get new tenants fast. Burrows out in an open fence line, by contrast, we will often tell you to leave alone.

Remington is a small town on the Rappahannock, and the river runs its wildlife calendar. The bottom farmland around town stays wet and rich, the wooded riverbanks hold raccoons and opossums in numbers, and the town's older homes — many of them standing since the railroad made Remington a shipping point — give those animals tall chimneys, tired soffits, and crawlspaces a short walk from the water. Spring floods push riverbank animals uphill into town foundations; summer sends skunks under every porch on the low streets; fall moves the whole population toward winter dens in attics and outbuildings.

Around the town, the farm country takes over the pattern: raccoons in barn lofts along the river road, groundhogs (woodchucks, in Fauquier speech) in the fence lines and under equipment sheds, bats in the farmhouse attics up the lanes. Remington sits close to the Culpeper line and the Brandy Station battlefield ground, and the open, historic farmland in every direction means there is no edge where the wildlife stops — our work here is about making your structures the one place on the landscape that is closed.
Remington.extendedBody:
River town housing, river bottom pressure

Remington's homes were built in railroad time — wood-frame, pier or stone foundations, additions across a century — and they stand lower and closer to wet ground than most Fauquier housing. That combination is why the crawlspace matters as much as the attic here: skunks and opossums den under the low porches and in the open foundation voids, while raccoons work the chimneys above. We inspect both ends of a Remington house on the first visit, because excluding an animal from the roof while the foundation stands open is half a job, and the river will supply a replacement tenant by the next season.

Farm work around Remington

Out the lanes, the calls are woodchucks under sheds and barn banks, raccoons splitting the year between barn lofts and farmhouse chimneys, and bats in the big farmhouse attics. Our operators hold a Commercial Nuisance Animal Permit (CNAP) issued by the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources. Virginia's rabies-vector species — raccoons and skunks — are handled by exclusion and sealing rather than relocation, and on farm properties we plan the work as a route: which structure the animals use first, which they fall back to, and what has to close so the route ends at your buildings instead of running through them.

Reading a Remington property

Chimney and roofline, then foundations and crawlspace vents at grade, then porches and outbuildings, with an eye on how high the river's influence reaches — burrow lines and debris marks often show exactly where flood-season animals travel. If your property takes water, we will say so plainly and build the sealing plan around it, because hardware that drowns every spring is not a seal.

faqs.q: An opossum has moved in under our Catlett porch. Is it a problem?
faqs.a: Usually a modest one, with one real exception. Opossums are quiet tenants — they do not dig like skunks or chew like raccoons — but a porch void that hosts an opossum this year advertises itself to skunks and raccoons next. We remove the opossum, then screen the porch perimeter with buried wire so the void stops existing as far as wildlife is concerned. If the opossum is only passing through the yard at night, we will tell you to leave it be; they eat ticks and carrion and ask very little.

faqs.q: Our farmhouse chimney gets raccoons every spring. Why ours?
faqs.a: Because an uncapped flue over a warm house, a short run from Cedar Run's woods, is the best den site in the neighbourhood — and raccoons remember and return to proven dens, with daughters denning near where they were raised. The fix is not the spring removal; it is the cap and the roofline sealing done with it. Once the flue is capped properly and the soffit gaps are closed, the family line moves on to somebody else's chimney. We also check the barn loft on the same visit, because on a Catlett farm the chimney and the loft are usually chapters of the same story.

Catlett is Cedar Run country — a railroad village in southern Fauquier where the creek bottoms, the pasture, and the old farmhouses all run together. Cedar Run and its branches thread past the village toward Calverton and Casanova, and the animals follow the water: raccoons denning in farmhouse chimneys and barn lofts, skunks under the porches of the older village homes, opossums in every outbuilding with a gap at the grade beam, and woodchucks working the fence lines and the sunny banks along the run. The housing here is farm housing — built practical, added onto for a century, and full of the junctions and voids that wildlife reads as floor plans.

The village's newer side tells the growth story of southern Fauquier: subdivisions and commuter homes spreading out from the Catlett crossroads toward the Prince William line, built fast against old pasture. Those homes get the suburban list — squirrels at the soffits, raccoons in the chimneys each spring, moles in the new lawns — while standing within sight of barns where the same species have lived for generations. Our Catlett inspections cover whichever version of the problem your property has, and plenty of properties here have both.
Catlett.extendedBody:
Cedar Run's animals and the farmhouses along it

The creek bottoms around Catlett never dry out as habitat — the wooded corridors along Cedar Run connect the farms, so a raccoon population is never really removed from a property, only excluded from its buildings. That is why our farm work here is sequenced: the house den is cleared and the flue capped, the barn loft entries are closed, and porch and outbuilding voids are screened, in one plan, so the animals' route through your structures ends everywhere at once. Farmhouses get a fabric-respecting version of the same work as any historic home — these places have stood since before the railroad, and their chimneys and eaves deserve better than foam and hope.

Rules we work under in Fauquier County

Our operators hold a Commercial Nuisance Animal Permit (CNAP) issued by the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources — that is the credential Virginia requires for this work. Raccoons and skunks are rabies-vector species here, handled by exclusion and sealing; an animal acting strangely in daylight, anywhere along the run, is a keep-your-distance call and we will tell you who else needs to hear about it. Bats, common in the farmhouse attics along the creek, are exclusion only, timed around the maternity season.

New homes against old pasture

For Catlett's newer subdivisions, the inspection is a roofline one: soffit returns where the canopy reaches, uncapped or poorly capped flues, and the deck voids that skunks claim in their first spring. New construction near old habitat gets its first wildlife lesson early — usually a raccoon mother in a chimney the first April — and the sealing done then, across the whole roofline rather than at the one hole, is what keeps the lesson from repeating annually.
